bib.title: Video-ChatGPT: Towards Detailed Video Understanding via Large Vision and Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Video-ChatGPT: Towards Detailed Video Understanding via Large Vision and Language Models", Maaz, Rasheed, Khan, Khan. ACL 2024 (Long Papers), pp. 12585–12602.

COVERAGE: All 18 of 18 pages, 43,730 of 43,730 chars. That covers the main text, Limitations, Risks, references (skimmed) and the appendix (pp. 12–18). The appendix is only qualitative example figures, with no extra numbers.

**The ACL version never states how many frames it samples (T), the input resolution, or the visual-token count.** It only gives the formula, T+N tokens. Any frame or token number in the note, such as "100 frames" or "356 tokens", would have to come from the repo or arXiv version. It cannot be cited to this PDF.

CLAIMS
- claim: Frames are encoded one at a time by CLIP ViT-L/14. Spatial pooling gives one token per frame, temporal pooling gives one token per patch position, and the two sets are concatenated. A single linear layer projects them into the LLM.
  number: (T+N) tokens; N = h×w; p = 14
  setup: CLIP ViT-L/14 from LLaVA; Vicuna-v1.1 7B
  quote: "Frame-level embeddings are average-pooled along the spatial dimension to obtain a video-level temporal representation ti ∈ RT ×D ... average-pooled along the temporal dimension to yield the video-level spatial representation zi ∈ RN ×D" and "vi = [ti zi] ∈ R(T +N )×D"
  where: p.3
- claim: Only the linear projection is trained; the encoder and LLM stay frozen. Training is cheap.
  number: 3 epochs, lr 2e-5, batch 32, ~3 h on 8 A100 40GB
  setup: LLaVA 7B initialisation, 100K pairs
  quote: "We only update the linear layer projecting the video features to the LLMs' input space ... training took around 3 hours on 8 A100 40GB GPUs."
  where: p.7
- claim: The training data is 100K video-instruction pairs built on ActivityNet-200 captions. About 30% are human-enriched captions and 70% are semi-automatic. The semi-automatic pipeline uses Katna keyframes, BLIP-2 frame captions and GRiT dense captions, filtered against Tag2Text tags (confidence 0.7). GPT-3.5 then merges the captions and writes the QA pairs. Training on the combined set scored best.
  number: 100,000; 30%/70%; average 2.28 human-only / 2.34 auto-only / 2.38 combined
  quote: "one with human annotations (30% of our data) and one with semi-automatic annotations (70%)"
  where: p.8 (pipeline p.5–6; Table 3 p.9)
- claim: The authors' own benchmark (ActivityNet-200 test set) is scored by GPT-3.5 on a 1–5 scale across five aspects. Video-ChatGPT leads but the margins are small. Temporal understanding is the weakest aspect for every model and ties with LLaMA Adapter.
  number: Correctness 2.40 vs Video Chat 2.23; Temporal 1.98 vs 1.94/1.98/1.82
  setup: all 7B models
  quote: "Temporal Understanding 1.94 1.98 1.82 1.98"; "assigns a relative score to the generated predictions ... on a scale of 1-5"
  where: p.7–8 (Table 1)
- claim: Zero-shot open-ended QA is also GPT-judged, reporting both accuracy and a 1–5 score. Video-ChatGPT is highest on all four datasets.
  number: MSVD 64.9/3.3 (Video Chat 56.3); MSRVTT 49.3/2.8 (45.0); TGIF 51.4/3.0 (FrozenBiLM 41.0); ActivityNet 35.2/2.8 (LLaMA Adapter 34.2)
  quote: "Video-ChatGPT 64.9 3.3 49.3 2.8 51.4 3.0 35.2 2.8"; "employing GPT-assisted evaluation"
  where: p.8 (Table 2)
- claim: Swapping the judge for Vicuna-1.5 13B keeps the model ranking but shifts the absolute scores, so scores from different judges are not comparable.
  number: Consistency 3.09 under Vicuna vs 2.37 under GPT-3.5
  quote: "Consistency 2.95 2.67 3.09"
  where: p.9 (Table 4)

LIMITS:
- The authors concede two failures: "challenging to understand subtle temporal relationships in long videos (> 2 min)" and "difficulty recognizing the details of small objects" (p.9).
- No human validation of the GPT judge.
- The "blind test" covers only 50 videos, and it checks whether the training data is distinguishable, not the scorer. People told human-made from automatic QA pairs apart only 52% of the time (p.9).
- No ablation of the pooling design, frame count or adapter. The paper only says a simple adapter "gives competitive performance" with no table.
- No audio or transcript input, so it is visual-only.
- No variance or confidence intervals, and the margins are small.
- The benchmark and the training data both come from ActivityNet-200, which risks in-domain advantage.
- Dated: GPT-3.5 as judge, 7B Vicuna-v1.1, mid-2023 baselines.

BUILDS ON:
- LLaVA (Liu et al., 2023): base model and visual encoder.
- CLIP (Radford et al., 2021, ICML).
- Vicuna (Chiang et al., 2023).
- ViFi-CLIP (Rasheed et al., 2023, CVPR): the temporal pooling idea.
- VideoChat (Li et al., 2023b, arXiv): main baseline.
- BLIP-2 (Li et al., 2023a), GRiT (Wu et al., 2022), Tag2Text (Huang et al., 2023), Katna (KeplerLab, 2019).
- FrozenBiLM (Yang et al., 2022).
- ActivityNet (Heilbron et al., 2015, CVPR).

CODE: none in the paper. Training prompt template (p.4): "USER: <Instruction> <Vid-tokens> Assistant:"

FIGURES:
- Figure 1, p.4, "Architecture of Video-ChatGPT ... averaging frame-level features across temporal and spatial dimensions respectively." It shows the two pooling axes faster than the equations do.
- Figure 3, p.6, the semi-automatic pipeline, is a second choice for the data section.

PROBLEMS: Extraction was clean, with no embedded instructions. The PDF has no frame-count or resolution details, as noted above.
